text: Last cycle, when investors were getting their heads around Defi, there was a very simple question that came up on the podcast with SBF and Odd lots. The question was, where does the yield come from? So I want to ask a similar question. Many of these crypto balance sheet companies are trading anywhere between two to five times the value of the underlying coins that they hold. So the question is, where does the premium come from? Why should investors pay more than the value of the coins that you hold?
speaker: A

text: It's a great question. So the way that we think about it, and I have to give credit to our wonderful IR guy for kind of coming up with this viewpoint, but what you actually do is you want to take the NAV and you want to separate it. You want to do a kind of a sum of the parts analysis, if you will. So you actually just value the coins on the balance sheet as one, because a dollar is a dollar, right? But then what you want to do is you want to look at the expected or your view of the expected future growth rates in those coins on the balance sheet. So in the same way that you might pay a PE to a company that is growing earnings, and nowadays you pay quite a pretty large multiple there, you would ascribe some value to the accumulation component in the future. Because if, if I could buy one Solana today and it's just going to be one sold forever, then I would just pay $1 for that. But if I could buy something that would be one sol today, and then two sol the next day, and then three sol the next day, you would be willing to Pay more than one SOL today. Basic Finance 101 present value stuff. And so that's kind of how we think about it. We separate the NAV to its current value and then this future projection. And we think that kind of evaluation framework makes a lot of sense.

The asset wicks down 50% in a day and you get liquidated and then the next day it's up 40%. But like too bad you're out. Right. Versus with unsecured debt. It's simply an obligation of the company.
